Modal soup?

Ah… very good, Laitch. Yup, I’d say this tune is a very interesting variation of Brian O‘Lynn’s. I’m not suggesting it was intentional; I think many tunes that are variations of existing tunes are composed without the intention or even the conscious knowledge of the tune that it is a variant of. Tom Doorly, of Danu, wrote a tune called “Are You Ready Yet?” that is as close to “Major Harrison’s Fedora” as this tune is to “Brian O’Lynn’s.” I never asked him, but I doubt it was intentional.

The Rooms of Dooagh

Another closely related tune called “The Short Grass” here: https://thesession.org/tunes/3058

In the sleeve notes of Mary MacNamara’s solo album, Jackie Small informs us that this tune was named after “a cave system in the hills between Maghera and Tulla,” East Clare. Maeve Donnelly and Peadar O’Loughlin recorded it as Pat Canny’s Jig. Pat was Paddy Canny’s father.

↳ Posted by Ann Viviano on June 27th, 2020.

Re: The Rooms Of Dooagh

I was just revisiting this tune today after a long absence, having listened to the recording by Paddy Canny and Peter O‘Loughlin on Friends of Note. I noticed that, compared to, say, the first version here, they play f# throughout, instead of f# in the first part and f natural in the second part. It’s interesting that all of the other East Clare players (Mary & Andrew MacNamara, Martin Hayes, Pat O’Connor, and Martin O’Brien) play the naturals, though, presumably, Paddy Canny would have been their source (with the tune sometimes bearing his father’s name). I would guess that he must have played it both ways.

Another interesting little difference in the Canny/O’Loughlin version is that in the first part, instead of the octave jump from G to g prior to the f#, they only jump up to e.

↳ Posted by GaryAMartin on July 16th, 2020.

X:6: Julia Clifford’s / Petticoat Loose / Rooms Of Dooagh

This is an interesting version of the jig that I learned from a tape of Julia and Billy Clifford. Since I got it as a gan ainm, I simply call it Julia Clifford’s. But turns out there’s an interesting title that’s been put on it and not once. Petticoat Loose.

There’s a pretty great documentary from the ITMA video series Drawing From the Well in which the Hurley sisters research the story of Petticoat Loose and the tunes that got this title. Turns out, the now-standard G major jig popularly known as Petticoat Loose had probably been converted from a minor tune of the same name. Which, in turn, could’ve been converted from the tune of the song Teidhir Abhaile Riú. Which, in turn… We could go on like this for ages. What’s interesting though, is that this particular jig gets an honourable mention and a short fragment of a Denis Murphy recording from the archives is played.

Whether or not this tune actually belongs to the same family of tunes as the better-known “Petticoat Loose” in G is up for debate (probably not?), but versions of it can be found titled thus in O’Neill’s 1001 and in Johnny O’Leary of Sliabh Luachra (although in case of Johnny it was also titled Con Carthy’s on one of his recordings).

The second part of this jig is nearly identical to some of the versions of Bryan O’Lynn / Ducks In the Oats / Scully Casey’s jig, which adds yet another layer of inheritance. I love how dramatically the first part in Julia’s version develops even better, though.

Fun fact: I took some liberties in deciding whether it’s c or c-sharp in some places since some of these in-between fiddle notes are open to interpretation, and then I went and listened to Johnny O’Leary playing this tune – only to discover he dropped a massive C# on the whole thing! One-row playing style something something? More versions potential!

Here’s the documentary on Petticoat Loose:
https://youtu.be/-LTKWgQgMO0

Re: The Rooms Of Dooagh

RE: 22 years ago; key(s) and significance of the f# …notes on modality;

If anything this tune revolves, on the whole, in the home keys of C and A (in part 2):
I can’t see -hear!- where D fits in here (except as a “suspended melodic cadence”, creating tension).

GaryAMartin, 6 years ago, observed that
Paddy Canny & Peter O’Loughlin, inter allies, play an all-f#-version (or versions).

Although C is an unusual key in Irish music, and lydian an even more unusual mode in this tradition, i suggest this tune is simply, at least in some of its rendition, a rare example of a C Lydian tune in Irish traditional music.

Foot note:
Modal and tonal ambiguity is a key (:-)) aspect of the Irish melodic tradition; it is a powerful and productive compositional device. This is why problems abound -and arguments arise- when we try to attribute a key autoritatively. In any case, the music came first and the jargon or concepts second (they are secondary) in this field.
